Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS)

Source: R/nmds.r
nmds.Rd

Ordinates samples from their distances, for plotting beta diversity, by placing them so that their distances on the plot are in the same rank order as the distances in dm, as nearly as possible. Uses the SMACOF algorithm of scikit-learn's non-metric MDS(), ported to parallel C that works from dm directly, with far less time and memory.

Usage

nmds(
  dm,
  n_axes = 2L,
  n_starts = 4L,
  max_iters = 1000L,
  tol = 1e-07,
  ties = "primary",
  seed = 0L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

dm

A dist object, such as from beta_div() or bray(), or a symmetric numeric matrix of distances. Must not contain NAs or negative values.

n_axes

The number of dimensions. Default: 2

n_starts

The number of random starts to run after the start from the PCoA solution, from 0 to 1000. Default: 4

max_iters

The maximum number of SMACOF iterations for each start. Default: 1000

tol

Each start stops once an iteration lowers the raw stress by no more than tol times the sum of squared distances on the plot (i.e., Kruskal's stress-1, squared, improves by less than about tol). Default: 1e-7

ties

How to treat tied distances in dm: "primary" (the default) lets them have different distances on the plot; "secondary" gives them equal disparities, as scikit-learn does. See "Ties and zeros" below.

seed

An integer seed for the random starts. Default: 0

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A numeric matrix with one row per sample and one column per dimension, named "NMDS1", "NMDS2", etc., as described in "Ordination result" below. method is "nmds"; eig and prop are NA, as NMDS has no eigenvalues. Then come:

  • stress: Kruskal's stress-1 of the solution, from 0 (a perfect rank order) to 1.

  • converged: TRUE if the best start stopped because a plain step met tol, FALSE if it stopped at max_iters.

  • n_iters: The number of SMACOF iterations the best start ran.

  • n_starts: The number of random starts run.

  • best_start: Which start gave the solution: 0 for the PCoA start, else the random start's number.

  • n_best: How many starts (of n_starts + 1) ended within 0.1% of the lowest stress. If it is 1, other starts might still find lower stress: try more.

  • ties: The approach to ties used, "primary" or "secondary".

With fewer than two samples there is nothing to fit: the result has no columns, stress is 0, and no starts are run.

Details

Which ordination?

pcoa(), mds(), and nmds() all place the samples in n_axes dimensions from dm. pcoa() (classical scaling) is exact and fast, and has eigenvalues and "variance explained", but it fits the squared distances after double centering, so large distances dominate, and non-Euclidean distances such as Bray-Curtis lose part of their structure to negative eigenvalues. mds() (metric MDS) fits the distances themselves, in their own units, so that distances on the plot can be read as the data's, with stress saying how well. nmds() fits only their rank order, which suits distances whose values matter less than their order, such as the saturated Bray-Curtis values of very different samples; it is the usual choice for community data. mds() and nmds() iterate from several starts, the first of them the PCoA solution, and so take longer than pcoa().

Method

NMDS minimizes Kruskal's stress-1, \(\sqrt{\sum(d_{ij} - \hat{d}_{ij})^2 / \sum d_{ij}^2}\), where \(d_{ij}\) are the distances between points on the plot, and the disparities \(\hat{d}_{ij}\) are the closest values to them (in least squares) that are in the same order as the distances in dm, found by isotonic regression. It is at most 1, as constant disparities are allowed.

Each start minimizes stress with SMACOF (de Leeuw, 1977; Borg & Groenen, 2005), as scikit-learn's non-metric smacof() does: the first iteration uses the distances in dm as disparities, and each later one fits them by isotonic regression; disparities are scaled so that their squares sum to the number of pairs; then the Guttman transform \(\Gamma\) moves the points. A start stops when its raw stress (the numerator above) falls by no more than tol times the denominator in one iteration, or after max_iters iterations. This rule is relative to the sum of squared distances, not to the stress itself, so a nearly perfect fit (stress-1 below about 0.01) stops while stress can still fall noticeably in relative terms; a smaller tol helps there. At the default tol, on typical data, stress ends within about 0.01-0.1% of its converged value, and points within about 1-5% of the configuration's spread of their converged positions; tol = 1e-8 cuts the stress error about tenfold and the displacement about threefold, for about 1.5 times the iterations.

Relaxed steps. To converge in fewer iterations, when k > 1, iterations after the first move the points twice as far as the Guttman transform would: \(X \leftarrow 2\Gamma(X) - X\), the relaxed update of de Leeuw and Heiser (1980). \(\Gamma\) doesn't depend on the scale of \(X\), so relaxed steps don't converge in that one direction (they flip the scale back and forth), nor at all when n_axes = 1, where \(\Gamma\) only depends on the order of the points. So a start takes relaxed steps only until one makes no more than tol progress, then plain steps until a plain step does (or until max_iters, whose last step is always plain), and n_axes = 1 uses plain steps throughout. The configuration returned and measured thus always comes from a plain step: it is a fixed point of \(\Gamma\) to within tol, and its stress is what plain steps reach from the same start. Relaxed steps typically save about half the iterations, but can end in a different local minimum than plain steps would.

In one dimension, SMACOF stops at the first order of the points that is a fixed point, which is often not the best one: random starts (n_starts) are the way to search for better ones.

Ties and zeros

Beta diversity distances are often tied, e.g. at 1 for every pair of samples with no taxa in common. With ties = "primary" (Kruskal's primary approach, as in vegan::metaMDS()), tied distances only have to stay in order with the other distances: on the plot, they may differ from each other. With "secondary" (as in scikit-learn), tied distances get one shared disparity, the mean of their distances on the plot, so the solution tries to make them equal too; this is a stronger requirement, so its stress is higher. Heavily tied data (e.g. Jaccard or Bray-Curtis on few taxa or rarefied counts) have many local minima of similar stress, and benefit from more n_starts; see n_best.

Distances count as tied when they are within \(10^{-15}\) times the largest distance of the first of their group (sorted increasingly), which absorbs rounding error in how they were computed.

Pairs with a distance of exactly 0, such as duplicate samples, have a disparity of 0 with either approach, as in scikit-learn: they are pulled towards the same point. (Under the primary approach, a zero would otherwise just be the smallest tie, free to take any small distance on the plot; but identical samples should coincide.) So when dm has no zeros, stress with ties = "primary" equals vegan::metaMDS()'s stress for the same configuration; when it has zeros, it is higher.

SMACOF only finds a local minimum of stress. So:

  1. The first start is the PCoA solution, from pcoa(). (An axis without a positive eigenvalue gets small random coordinates instead.)

  2. Then come n_starts random starts, with coordinates uniform on [0, 1).

  3. The start whose final configuration has the lowest stress-1 is kept; if several tie exactly, the earliest. Its configuration is centered, rotated to its principal axes, and scaled so that the distances between points have the same root mean square as the distances in dm. Each axis is flipped so that its coordinate with the largest absolute value is positive (the first such sample, if several are within a relative \(10^{-8}\) of it).

Differences from scikit-learn

With plain steps only (an internal setting used by the tests) and ties = "secondary", a start follows scikit-learn's iterations from the same starting configuration to within rounding error: the raw stress of every iteration agrees to about \(10^{-13}\), relatively. (Rarely more: when points nearly coincide, scikit-learn's distance formula rounds their tiny distances to 0, which can change an iteration count.) Otherwise:

  • scikit-learn takes plain Guttman steps; nmds() takes relaxed ones (see above).

  • scikit-learn's defaults are max_iter = 300 and eps = 1e-6; for a good fit (stress-1 of 0.05, squared 0.0025), 1e-6 stops while stress still falls by 0.04% per iteration. nmds() defaults to max_iters = 1000 and tol = 1e-7.

  • scikit-learn always uses the secondary approach to ties; nmds() uses the primary one unless ties = "secondary".

  • scikit-learn runs n_init random starts (init = "random", its current default) or one start from classical MDS (init = "classical_mds"); nmds() runs both kinds.

  • scikit-learn ranks starts by the stress of the last iteration, measured with the previous iteration's disparities; nmds() ranks them by stress-1 with disparities fitted to each start's final configuration, which is the value reported, and is never higher.

  • scikit-learn returns the configuration as SMACOF leaves it; nmds() centers, rotates, scales, and flips it as described above. None of that changes the stress.

  • scikit-learn stops when stress falls by less than eps; nmds() stops when it falls by no more than tol, so that tol = 0 stops once stress no longer falls.

  • scikit-learn's tie tolerance is an absolute \(10^{-15}\); nmds()'s is relative to the largest distance, so that results don't depend on the units of dm.

  • scikit-learn computes distances on the plot with the expansion \(|x|^2 - 2 x \cdot y + |y|^2\), and replaces distances of 0 by \(10^{-5}\) in the Guttman transform; nmds() computes them directly, and leaves out pairs at distance 0, whose contribution \(r_{ij}(x_i - x_j)\) is 0 either way.

  • The random starts come from seed, not from R's or NumPy's random number generators, so set.seed() has no effect, and R's random number stream is left untouched.

Speed and memory

dm's pairs are sorted by distance once, and the order is shared by all starts: 4 bytes and 1 bit per pair. Each start that runs at the same time needs 8 more bytes per pair, plus \(256 n k\) bytes. With ties = "primary", it also needs 4 bytes per pair for its own order within tie groups, and scratch space of 12 bytes per pair in the largest tie group (more for several threads, but at most a quarter of all the pairs' worth in all). Besides one copy of dm as a plain vector of doubles, nothing of size \(n \times n\) is formed, and distances on the plot are recomputed from the coordinates as needed. Sorting the pairs at the outset takes time proportional to \(n^2 \log n\), and briefly needs 16 bytes per pair in its largest bucket (about \(N / 16384\) of the \(N\) pairs, for large data) for each thread.

Each SMACOF iteration makes two passes over the pairs, and so takes time proportional to \(n^2 k\), plus the isotonic regression, a pass on one thread. With ties = "primary", each iteration also re-sorts the distances within each group of tied ones, which is fast when they barely change, but on heavily tied data can cost several times the rest of the iteration (e.g. about 4 times, at 1 CPU, on Bray-Curtis of rarefied counts with 78 distinct values); groups are sorted in parallel, in up to 64 parts. ties = "secondary" avoids that cost.

Several starts run at once, one per thread, while their memory totals at most 1 GiB and one iteration takes under about \(2^{26}\) pairs of work (\(n\) up to about 11,500). Otherwise, starts run one at a time, with each iteration's passes over the pairs (and the re-sorting of tie groups) split across cpus threads, for data with at least \(2^{18}\) pairs (\(n\) of about 725). Long passes run in parts between checks for user interrupts.

dm may have at most 65,536 samples.

Reproducibility

The result, with all its attributes, is bit-identical from run to run, in new R sessions, and for any value of cpus, given the same dm, n_axes, n_starts, max_iters, tol, ties, and seed. Each start splits its sums into a fixed number of parts that depends only on the number of samples, and adds them in a fixed order; the sort order of the distances is a total order (tied distances keep their order in dm), and so is the order of each tie group's re-sort; and nothing depends on the BLAS library. dm is read as dm times a power of 2 that brings its largest value near 1, so dm * 2^p gives exactly the same result times \(2^p\), and neither tiny nor large scales overflow. (As for every ordination, distances above \(10^{150}\) are rejected.) Results can still differ in the last bits between computers or compilers, as for any floating point code.

n_axes larger than \(n - 1\) is reduced to \(n - 1\).

Ordination result

Every ordination function (pcoa(), pca(), rpca(), dbrda(), capda(), capscale(), mds(), nmds(), isomap(), tsne(), umap(), and so dist_ord()) returns the same kind of object: a numeric matrix with one row per sample and one column per axis, so that it can go straight into a data frame. Rows are named after the samples, when the input has names. Columns are named after the method: "PCoA1", "PC1", "RPCA1", "dbRDA1" or "CAP1" (then "MDS1" for unconstrained axes), "MDS1", "NMDS1", "Isomap1", "TSNE1", "UMAP1", and so on.

Its attributes always begin with these three, in this order, each with one value per column:

  • method: The method's ID, e.g. "pcoa" or "nmds".

  • eig: Each axis's eigenvalue, on the method's own scale: pcoa() and isomap() give the eigenvalues of Gower's centered matrix (sums of squares); pca() and rpca() give variances, which are pcoa()'s divided by \(n - 1\) for \(n\) samples; and dbrda() and capscale() follow vegan, which also divides by \(n - 1\) when any distance is 4 or more. NA for mds(), nmds(), tsne(), and umap(), which have no eigenvalues.

  • prop: The proportion of the total variance (or inertia) that each axis explains. Unlike eig, it is comparable between methods, so use it to label axes. NA where it isn't defined.

Attributes particular to the method follow them. The matrix has class "ecodive_ord" (as well as "matrix"), so that print() lists the other attributes by name rather than in full, and plot() draws the samples on the first two axes, labelled from the attributes, with any loadings, constraints and centroids on top (see plot.ecodive_ord()). plot(ord, "Species", iris) colours the samples by a column of metadata. Subsetting with [, or as.data.frame(), gives a plain matrix or data frame without the attributes.

References

Kruskal, J. B. (1964). Nonmetric multidimensional scaling: A numerical method. Psychometrika, 29(2), 115-129. doi:10.1007/BF02289694

de Leeuw, J. (1977). Applications of convex analysis to multidimensional scaling. In J. R. Barra, F. Brodeau, G. Romier, & B. van Cutsem (Eds.), Recent Developments in Statistics (pp. 133-145). North Holland.

de Leeuw, J., & Heiser, W. J. (1980). Multidimensional scaling with restrictions on the configurations. In P. R. Krishnaiah (Ed.), Multivariate Analysis V (pp. 501-522). North Holland.

Borg, I., & Groenen, P. J. F. (2005). Modern Multidimensional Scaling: Theory and Applications (2nd ed.). Springer. doi:10.1007/0-387-28981-X

Pedregosa, F., et al. (2011). Scikit-learn: Machine learning in Python. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 12, 2825-2830. Examples

    dm  <- bray(iris[, 1:4])
    ord <- nmds(dm)
    plot(ord, 'Species', iris)

    head(ord)
#>          NMDS1       NMDS2
#> [1,] 0.1703377 -0.02307947

#> [6,] 0.1364458 -0.05359534
